title: Best Healthcare Jobs for College Students
summary: See the best healthcare jobs for college students, including duties, education requirements, average salary, and everything else you need to know
body_markdown:
Many healthcare roles only require a high school diploma or GED to get hired or start training, so they are open to anyone in college.


Most training and[certification programs](https://www.stepful.com/programs) are flexible enough to do while maintaining college coursework. Since some take only a few weeks to several months to complete, students can also do them during a summer break.


Healthcare pays college students better than the jobs they often do, like retail and food service. According to federal wage data, retail sales workers earn a median of[$17.10 an hour,](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/sales/retail-sales-workers.htm) food and beverage servers earn[$15.24](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/food-preparation-and-serving/food-and-beverage-serving-and-related-workers.htm) , medical assistants earn[$21.97,](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/medical-assistants.htm) and dental assistants earn[$23.11](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/dental-assistants.htm) .


College students can also benefit from the flexible hours that are built into many of these roles. Healthcare settings run around the clock, so work hours aren't limited to the usual 9 to 5. Evening, overnight, and weekend shifts are common in hospitals, assisted living facilities, and home health.


There's even more upside if you’re thinking about[healthcare as a career](https://www.stepful.com/post/jobs-in-healthcare-medical-field) . Time spent interacting with patients, learning clinical terminology, and building relationships with physicians and nurses will pay off on a graduate or med school application.


This guide covers 12 healthcare jobs that work well for college students. We’ll cover how long it takes to train, what each pays, how much flexibility it offers, how to get started, and how to decide which job makes the most sense for your major or career goals.


## Best Healthcare Jobs for College Students


Two important considerations come up when choosing a healthcare job you can do during college. You need to be able to train without missing school, and the work should build skills or offer other benefits that improve your future prospects.


Training for most of the roles below takes five months or less of part-time coursework, and several take a month or less to complete. Training programs are often designed for working adults, so they naturally offer part-time and evening classes.


In addition, all these jobs give you tangible skills you can use in the future. Working as a patient care technician or a scribe puts you in a clinical setting with real patients and experienced providers.


They can teach you skills and mentor you. And when you need letters of recommendation for the next step in your career, they’ll have something specific to say about you.


Job Training Time Hourly Pay (median unless noted) Flexibility Best For

Pay data for most of these jobs is the national median from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) as of May 2025. If BLS data was not available, we used a national average from Indeed.com.


*The BLS publishes one hourly median for nursing assistants and orderlies together, and one for EMTs and paramedics together, so these rates are extrapolated from the annual wage data they provide separately.


### 1) Medical Assistant


[Medical assistants](https://www.stepful.com/post/what-is-a-medical-assistant) (MAs) do both clinical and administrative tasks. They can take a patient’s vital signs and prep them for an exam or schedule an appointment and update medical records. They work mostly in physicians' offices, outpatient clinics, and hospitals.


The mix of clinical and administrative work makes this a great first job in healthcare because you learn a variety of skills and are critical to a healthcare team. This is a common role for people who are premed or who plan to become physician assistants (PAs).


There are many[part-time medical assistant programs](https://www.stepful.com/post/part-time-medical-assistant-program) and programs with[night classes](https://www.stepful.com/post/medical-assistant-programs-with-night-classes) for students taking classes during the day.


For example, Stepful’s[Online Certified Medical Assistant Program](https://www.stepful.com/medical-assistant) has both part-time and night-class options. It takes five months to complete and includes two live, 90-minute classes per week.


The program prepares students to earn the National Healthcareer Association’s[Certified Clinical Medical Assistant (CCMA) credential](https://www.stepful.com/post/certified-clinical-medical-assistant) .


- **Educational requirements and training time:** A high school diploma or GED is the only educational requirement, but most employers prefer training and certification.[Programs can run from](https://www.stepful.com/post/how-long-does-a-medical-assisting-program-last) five months for certificate programs to two years for degree programs.
- **Median pay:**[$21.97 per hour or $45,690 per year](https://www.stepful.com/medical-assistant-salaries/united-states)
- **Where they work:** Physicians' offices, outpatient care centers, hospitals. Learn more about[where medical assistants work here](https://www.stepful.com/post/where-do-medical-assistants-work) .
- **Schedule flexibility:** Moderate. Most clinic work is daytime and weekday, though urgent care and hospital-based roles have evening and weekend shifts.

### 2) Certified Nursing Assistant


[Certified Nursing Assistants](https://www.stepful.com/post/what-is-a-cna) , also called CNAs, provide hands-on care to patients in hospitals, nursing homes, and assisted living facilities. They bathe, feed, reposition patients, take vitals, and report changes to the nurses who supervise them.


[MAs and CNAs have many similarities in their jobs.](https://www.stepful.com/post/medical-assistant-vs-certified-nursing-assistant) However, if you’re considering nursing as a career, this is the best way to learn how a nursing floor actually operates.


- **Educational requirements and training time:** You need a high school diploma or GED to begin training.[Federal rules](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-483/subpart-D/section-483.152) require at least 75 hours of training, including 16 hours of supervised practical training, for aides working in Medicare- and Medicaid-certified facilities. States can and often do require more. Programs commonly run four to 12 weeks, and you typically must pass a state competency exam before working with patients. Learn more about[becoming a CNA here](https://www.stepful.com/post/how-to-become-a-cna) .
- **Median pay:**[$20.32 per hour or $42,260 per year](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/nursing-assistants.htm#tab-5)
- **Where they work:** Nursing and residential care facilities, and hospitals
- **Schedule flexibility:** Night and weekend shifts are widely available, and overnight shifts often pay more than the base wage. Flexibility is high because these facilities need workers 24/7.


### 3) Phlebotomist


[Phlebotomists](https://www.stepful.com/post/what-is-a-phlebotomist-and-what-do-they-do) draw blood for testing, transfusions, research, and donation, then label and log the samples. It's a skill you can learn quickly, and it puts you in a hospital, doctor’s office, or lab environment fast.


Phlebotomy is one of the easiest[entry-level healthcare jobs](https://www.stepful.com/post/entry-level-healthcare-jobs) to get into. Some programs offer online coursework, but hands-on training may be needed to meet certification, employer, or state requirements. Training length varies by program.


- **Educational requirements and training time:** You need a high school diploma or GED and a training course. Some programs can be completed in a month; others take longer. Some states require a license or certification, so check with your state health agency before enrolling in a training program.
- **Median pay:**[$21.75 per hour or $45,230 per year](https://www.stepful.com/post/phlebotomist-salary)
- **Where they work:** Hospitals, diagnostic labs, blood donation centers, physicians' offices
- **Schedule flexibility:** Early-morning shifts are common at hospitals, private labs, and mobile blood drives, so flexibility is high.


### 4) Medical Scribe


Scribes[shadow a physician](https://www.stepful.com/post/how-to-shadow-a-doctor) during patient visits and document the encounter in the electronic health records in real time. There's no direct patient care involved, but you do get to **** hear how doctors think through a diagnosis.


You’ll learn a lot of medical terminology and the charting system of different healthcare settings. Training is almost always done on the job by the employer.


This is a[great job for premed students](https://www.stepful.com/post/best-jobs-for-premed-students-and-med-school-gap-year) because you can learn by observing doctors and build relationships that can help with med school applications.


- **Educational requirements and training time:** A high school diploma or GED is required. Most employers train new scribes directly, usually over a few weeks of classroom and shadowing time, at no cost to you.
- **Average pay:**[$19.23 per hour](https://www.indeed.com/career/medical-scribe/salaries) , according to Indeed’s national medical scribe salary data updated September 20, 2026.
- **Where they work:** Emergency departments, specialty clinics, urgent care, and primary care offices
- **Schedule flexibility:** Shifts follow the physician you're assigned to, so an ER scribe can work nights and weekends, while a clinic scribe works weekday hours. Many scribe companies build schedules around student availability so that this job can be very flexible.


### 5) Patient Care Technician


A[patient care technician](https://www.stepful.com/post/patient-care-technician) (PCT) provides direct patient care, such as bathing, feeding, and helping patients get dressed. They may also do clinical tasks like drawing blood or running EKGs. That broader skill set gives them added flexibility because they can work in different settings.


Training programs are fairly quick and don’t typically require clinical hours. Stepful’s[Patient Care Technician Program](https://www.stepful.com/patient-care-tech) , for example, takes only eight weeks and prepares you to earn the NHA’s[Certified Patient Care Technician/Assistant (CPCT/A)](https://www.stepful.com/post/patient-care-technician-certifications) credential.


- **Educational requirements and training time:** You need a high school diploma or GED. Training can be on the job or through a certificate program. Training length varies from about a month for some certificate programs to two years for degree programs.
- **Average pay:**[$22.17 per hour](https://www.indeed.com/career/patient-care-technician/salaries) , according to Indeed data.
- **Where they work:** Hospitals, dialysis clinics, and long-term care facilities
- **Schedule flexibility:** PCTs are needed 24 hours a day, just like CNAs, so this job offers a lot of flexibility.


[Learn About Stepful's Online Patient Care Technician Program](https://www.stepful.com/patient-care-tech)


[Explore Program](https://www.stepful.com/patient-care-tech)


### 6) EKG Technician


EKG technicians hook patients up to electrocardiogram equipment, run the test, and prepare the report for a physician. They must know how to correctly place the monitoring leads to get an accurate picture of the heart.


It's a focused technical skill with a short learning curve, and it's especially good for students interested in cardiology or diagnostic imaging as a career. Most employers prefer certified technicians.


To be eligible for the NHA's[Certified EKG Technician](https://www.nhanow.com/certification/nha-certifications/certified-ekg-technician-%28cet%29) credential, you generally need a high school diploma or equivalent and either an EKG training program completed within the past five years or qualifying supervised work experience. Both pathways require proof that you have successfully performed at least 10 EKGs on live people.


- **Educational requirements and training time:** You need a high school diploma or GED. Certificate programs generally run a few weeks to a few months.
- **Average pay:** $[25.25 per hour](https://www.indeed.com/career/ekg-technician/salaries) , according to data from Indeed
- **Where they work:** Hospitals, cardiology practices, diagnostic centers
- **Schedule flexibility:** Moderate. Hospital cardiology departments run extended hours, but most testing is scheduled on weekdays.


### 7) Home Health Aide


[Home health aides](https://www.stepful.com/post/what-is-a-home-health-aide) help clients with bathing, dressing, meals, light housekeeping, and basic health monitoring, usually in the client's own home. Because the work happens one client at a time rather than on a hospital unit, the scheduling is very flexible.


In most states, you’ll need to complete a state-approved training program, pass an in-person skills assessment, and get certified. Stepful’s[Online Home Health Aide Program](https://www.stepful.com/training/home-health-aide) prepares you for state certification.


- **Educational requirements and training time:** You need a high school diploma or GED to begin training.[Federal rules](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-484/subpart-B/section-484.80) require at least 75 hours of training for aides working for Medicare- and Medicaid-certified agencies. States can and often do require more. This process takes from a few weeks to a few months depending on your state requirements.
- **Median pay:**[$17.21 per hour or $35,800 a year](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/home-health-aides-and-personal-care-aides.htm)
- **Where they work:** Clients' homes, group homes, care communities
- **Schedule flexibility:** Evenings, weekends, and short visits are standard, so flexibility is very high.


### 8) Emergency Medical Technician (EMT)


EMTs respond to 911 calls and assess patients. They provide basic life support and transport people to the hospital. This job requires a state-approved training course and certification.


Being an EMT is a common choice for people[hoping to become physician assistants (PAs)](https://www.stepful.com/post/best-jobs-to-do-before-pa-school) or doctors because you’re making decisions under pressure with almost no buffer between you and the patient.


- **Educational requirements and training time:** Training and certification vary, but most take three to six months. You'll need to pass the[National Registry](https://www.nremt.org/EMT/Certification) cognitive exam and a state skills evaluation.
- **Median pay:**[$21.38 per hour or $44,470 a year](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/emts-and-paramedics.htm#tab-5)
- **Where they work:** Ambulance services, fire departments, hospitals
- **Schedule flexibility:** Moderate. Shifts often run 12, 18, or 24 hours, which can free up whole weekdays. Nights, weekends, and holidays are part of the job.


### 9) Pharmacy Technician


[Pharmacy technicians help](https://www.stepful.com/post/what-is-a-pharmacy-technician) fill prescriptions, measure medication, manage inventory, and handle insurance claims under a pharmacist's supervision. They work in retail pharmacies and hospitals.[Training takes from four months to a year](https://www.stepful.com/post/how-long-it-takes-to-become-a-pharmacy-technician-length-of-school-training) , and you may need to be licensed in some states.


Stepful’s ASHP/ACPE-accredited[Pharmacy Technician Professional program](https://www.stepful.com/pharmacy-technician-professional) prepares you for national certification and is available in select states. The academic work is 100% online and is followed by mandatory, in-person clinical hours.


After your hands-on experience, Stepful provides job coaching to help you land a job in your area.


- **Educational requirements and training time:** You need a high school diploma or GED and training (on-the-job or a program). Most employers prefer certification. Requirements vary by state, so check your state board of pharmacy.
- **Median pay:**[$22.00 per hour or $45,750 a year](https://www.stepful.com/pharmacy-technician-salaries/united-states)
- **Where they work:** Retail pharmacies, hospitals, mail-order and specialty pharmacies
- **Schedule flexibility:** Retail pharmacies run long hours seven days a week, and evening and weekend shifts are routine, so schedules are often flexible.


[Learn about Stepful's 4-Month Online Pharmacy Technician Program](https://www.stepful.com/pharmacy-tech)[Explore Program](https://www.stepful.com/pharmacy-tech)


### 10) Dental Assistant


[Dental assistants](https://www.stepful.com/post/what-is-a-dental-assistant-what-do-they-do) prepare patients and instruments, hand tools to the dentist during procedures, take X-rays where state rules allow it, and handle sterilization. It's a great choice if you're considering dental hygiene or dental school, and it pays near the top of this list.


Each state has its own requirements for training, certification, and licensing. Stepful’s[Dental Assistant Program](https://www.stepful.com/dental-assistant) takes four months to complete and prepares students for the Dental Assisting National Board’s Radiation Health and Safety (RHS) exam.


- **Educational requirements and training time:** Requirements vary by state. Some dental assistants train on the job, while others must complete an approved program or earn credentials for specific duties. Training can take from four months to a year and can be done online or at a community or technical college. Check your state requirements.
- **Median pay:**[$23.11 per hour or $48,070 a year](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/dental-assistants.htm)
- **Where they work:** Dentists' offices, specialty dental practices
- **Schedule flexibility:** Dental offices keep business hours, so flexibility is lower, but the schedule is more regular and reliable.


### 11) Medical Secretary/Medical Administrative Assistant


[Medical secretaries](https://www.stepful.com/post/medical-secretary) and[medical administrative assistants](https://www.stepful.com/post/medical-administrative-assistant) work at the front desk of a clinic, hospital, or doctor’s office. They check patients in, verify insurance, do scheduling, and answer phones.


You’ll learn how a practice runs, how insurance actually functions, and how to talk to patients who are anxious or frustrated. It’s good pay with moderately flexible hours that doesn’t require any special training or certification.


- **Educational requirements and training time:** A high school diploma or GED is usually enough, with on-the-job training provided. No certificate or license required.


- **Median pay:**[$22.08 per hour or $45,930 a year](https://www.stepful.com/medical-administrative-assistant-salaries/united-states)
- **Where they work:** Physicians' offices, clinics, hospitals, dental practices
- **Schedule flexibility:** Most offices are open during regular business hours, so you'll have less flexibility but a more regular schedule. Jobs at hospitals or urgent clinics often include nights and weekends.


[Learn about Stepful’s Online Medical Administrative Assistant program](https://www.stepful.com/medical-admin)[Explore Program](https://www.stepful.com/medical-admin)


### 12) Dispensing Optician


Dispensing opticians measure customers for eyeglasses and contact lenses, help them choose frames, write up lab orders, and adjust and repair eyewear. Most work in optometrists' offices or retail settings, which means retail-style hours including evenings and weekends.


This is one of the best[entry-level healthcare jobs](https://www.stepful.com/post/entry-level-healthcare-jobs) because it doesn’t require much specialized training. Some states require a license, and some don't.


- **Educational requirements and training time:** A high school diploma or GED is the typical entry point, with on-the-job training or an apprenticeship. Licensing requirements vary by state and may include an exam, an approved program, and/or supervised work experience.
- **Median pay:**[$22.72 per hour or $47,260 a year](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/opticians-dispensing.htm)
- **Where they work:** Optometrists' offices, retailers
- **Schedule flexibility:** Moderate. Part-time positions are common, and stores stay open evenings and weekends, but you're working set store hours rather than picking up shifts.


## Which Healthcare Jobs for College Students Offer the Most Flexible Schedules?


There are two ways to look at scheduling.


A work setting that is open nights, weekends, and holidays, like a hospital or assisted living facility, offers shift work. That lets you change your work schedule when your school schedule changes. You can also work at times you wouldn’t have class, like weekends.


A work setting that has regular business hours, like a doctor’s or dentist’s office, won’t offer changing work patterns, but it will give you a regular schedule you can rely on. For example, you can work early mornings and have afternoons free for school.


Here’s where the jobs on this list land on the flexibility question:


- **Home health aide (HHA).** Visit-based work in clients' homes means evenings, weekends, and short blocks are all normal.
- **Certified nursing assistant (CNA) and patient care technician (PCT).** Hospitals and nursing homes staff 24 hours a day, so workers are needed evenings, weekends, and holidays.
- **Phlebotomist.** Early-morning shifts are common at labs and blood drives, which work for a daytime class schedule.
- **Pharmacy technician.** Retail pharmacies are open long hours seven days a week, so you can get a regular shift during nontraditional hours.
- **Medical scribe.** The schedule depends entirely on the physician you're assigned to, but scribe employers are used to scheduling students.
- **EMT.** Long shifts free up full days, but a 12- or 24-hour commitment is harder to fit around a scattered class schedule.
- **Medical assistant.** Most medical assistants work in doctors’ offices with traditional hours. That setting also offers part-time hours. However, many medical assistants work in hospitals and urgent care settings that are 24/7 and provide shift work.
- **EKG technician, dental assistant, medical admin assistant, and dispensing optician.** Hours are more traditional, though part-time schedules are common.


One thing to note about healthcare work: Hospitals **** and other 24/7 settings frequently pay more for overnight and weekend hours. Working the shifts nobody else wants is a great way to make more money and keep your days free for school.


## How to Choose the Right Healthcare Job for Your Major or Career Goals


If you’re going to spend your time training for and doing a job in healthcare, choose one that will benefit you in the long run. These jobs offer clinical experience and professional connections that are, in many ways, just as valuable as a paycheck.


- **Premed and pre-PA students:** Medical assistant, Medical scribe, and EMT are the roles that give you the most direct exposure to patients, physician decision-making, and emergency care. Scribing puts you next to a doctor for every patient encounter. Medical assisting is a great way to get[clinical experience for medical school](https://www.stepful.com/post/can-working-as-a-medical-assistant-help-you-get-into-med-school) .
- **Pre-nursing students:** CNA and patient care technician roles build the patient care hours nursing programs want to see and teach you how a hospital unit functions.
- **Pre-pharmacy students:** Pharmacy technician experience is directly relevant to PharmD applications and is the closest preview of the job itself.
- **Pre-dental students:** Dental assistant work puts you chairside for procedures and naturally leads to dental hygiene or dental school.
- **Undecided health majors:** Medical assistant and phlebotomist give you broad, transferable clinical exposure without locking you into a specialty.


## How to Get Started in a Healthcare Job as a College Student


1. **Figure out which certificate or training program fits your schedule and your budget.** Compare program length, cost, and whether classes are live, self-paced, or evening.[Stepful trains students online](https://www.stepful.com/programs) for roles including medical assistant, patient care technician, pharmacy technician, and dental assistant, with programs running from eight weeks to five months and flexible class options.
2. **Check whether your school hires students directly.** Start with your campus health center, the student employment office, and any hospital system affiliated with your university. These employers already expect to work around exam weeks.[University of Iowa Health Care](https://uihc.org/student-opportunities-ui-health-care) , for example, lists patient care technician, nursing assistant, and phlebotomy technician among its student opportunities and advertises flexible scheduling so students can balance school and work.
3. **Complete the coursework and any required clinical or externship hours.** Add your healthcare job training into your regular class and study schedule and knock it out. In many cases, you can use a summer or holiday break to complete training.
4. **Get certified or licensed if your role and state require it.** Before enrolling, confirm that the program meets your state’s requirements and qualifies you for the certification exam you plan to take. It’s always a good idea to check the role you’re working toward against your state’s health department rules and regulations to make sure you know what is and isn’t required.
5. **Apply for jobs and tell employers your class schedule upfront.** Healthcare managers hire students all the time and would much rather know your availability in the interview than find out during finals week.


## Healthcare Jobs for College Students FAQs


**What are the best-paying healthcare jobs for college students?**
Among the roles you can train for in a few months, EKG technicians lead at $25.25 an hour on average, followed by dental assistants at $23.11 and dispensing opticians at $22.72. Patient care technicians, medical admin assistants, and pharmacy technicians all pay around $22.00 per hour. Overnight and weekend shifts at a hospital can push CNA and patient care technician pay above the base median.


**What healthcare jobs can college students get with no certification?**
Medical scribe and medical administrative assistant are two roles that generally require only a high school diploma, with employer-provided training. Dispensing optician is available without certification in some states.


**What is the easiest healthcare job to get as a college student?**
Medical administrative assistant jobs have the lowest barrier, since there's no program to finish first. If you want clinical work, phlebotomy has the shortest training path at roughly a month.


**What healthcare jobs only require a high school diploma?**
All the jobs on this list require only a high school diploma or GED to get started. Many also require training programs or on-the-job training. Some require certification or licensing, but none of these require an associate’s or bachelor’s degree.


**Can I work in healthcare part-time while in school?**
Yes, and it's common. Hospitals, nursing homes, and home care agencies run 24 hours a day and staff heavily with part-time workers. These employers are used to accommodating employees who are in school.


**Which healthcare job is best if I want to go to pharmacy school?**
Pharmacy technician. You'll work directly under licensed pharmacists, learn the workflow and terminology, and gain experience PharmD programs recognize.


**Which healthcare job is best if I'm premed?**
Working as a medical assistant is a great way to get[clinical experience for medical school](https://www.stepful.com/post/clinical-experience-for-medical-school) . Being a medical scribe gives you the most physician exposure per hour worked because you document every patient encounter alongside a doctor. EMT is also a strong choice if you want hands-on patient care and can commit to long shifts.


**Do I need a car for any of these jobs?**
Home health aide work almost always requires reliable transportation, since you're traveling between clients' homes. Hospital-based roles like CNA, patient care technician, and phlebotomist are usually accessible by public transit if you're near a medical center.


**Will a healthcare job hurt my GPA?**
That depends on how many hours you work and how well you can balance work and school. Working 10 to 15 hours a week is not the same challenge as working 30-hour weeks of rotating night shifts. Start with fewer hours than you think you can handle and add more once you see how the semester goes.
